title: Children Creatively Against Anxiety (KIKAN): Pilot Study of an App Developed Using a Participatory Design Approach to Support Outpatient Psychotherapy for Childhood Anxiety Disorders
summary:
Background: Anxiety disorders are among the most common mental health problems in children. In many cases they can lead to lasting difficulties and limitations in various areas of life. Despite the proven effectiveness of psychotherapeutic interventions, many children do not receive adequate treatment or benefit insufficiently. Digital tools such as playful apps could increase the effectiveness of treatment and make it easier to collect therapy relevant subjective and physiological data in children’s everyday lives (so called Ecological Momentary Assessments, EMA).

Research Question: As part of the project KIKAN [“Kids Creatively Against Anxiety”], funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, a playful tablet app was co‑developed with children, caregivers, and therapists. The app is intended to be used in addition to standard outpatient psychotherapy for childhood anxiety disorders. It not only captures game related information but also gathers children’s everyday subjective well being and physiological measurements (via a smartband). In this study we will examine, alongside questionnaire-based measures of mental health symptoms (e.g., general, internally experienced, and anxiety-related complaints, quality of life) and therapeutic processes (e.g., self efficacy, therapeutic alliance), feasibility aspects and the acceptability of using the app in daily life and within outpatient therapy. 
We will examine the following research questions: Do children who use KIKAN in addition to outpatient psychotherapy show improvements in general, internally experienced, and anxiety related complaints that are comparable to the improvements seen with outpatient psychotherapy alone? Does quality of life increase over the course of KIKAN supported therapy to a comparable extent as it does with outpatient psychotherapy without KIKAN? How are changes in the most important therapeutic outcomes, other clinical measures, and therapy process variables related to the data generated by the app (gaming behavior, EMA, and acceptance of KIKAN)? Is the KIKAN app accepted by children, their caregivers, and therapists, and is the overall approach feasible?

Methodology: In a first study, approximately 30 children aged 6-12 years will be included. They will use the KIKAN app throughout their usually 12 weekly outpatient psychotherapy sessions for anxiety. The app contains child friendly, game like modules that are intended to convey effective therapeutic content.
Questionnaires assessing mental health symptoms (e.g., general, internally experienced, and anxiety-related complaints, quality of life, emotion regulation, self-efficacy) and the acceptability of the KIKAN app will be completed by children and caregivers at the following time points: baseline, start of the intervention, mid intervention evaluation, end of the intervention, and three months after the end of the intervention.
In addition, therapists will complete questionnaires on symptom severity and on the acceptability of the KIKAN app, and therapists and children will fill out process of therapy questionnaires in the context of each therapy session (e.g., self efficacy, therapeutic relationship). Feasibility indicators will also be recorded (e.g., recruitment numbers, use of the app, possible drop outs).
Furthermore, EMA data will be recorded at all time points (except three months after the end of the intervention) over a two‑week period. During these periods the children will wear a smartband that records physiological data (e.g., heart rate and sleep). Children and caregivers will answer daily questions about daily emotional states during these periods.

Hypotheses: 
1. Concerning the most important therapeutic outcomes. We hypothesize that:
- the children’s condition will improve over the course of the KIKAN-supported therapy, as indicated by a reduction in general complaints, internally experienced complaints, and anxiety symptoms, as well as an increase in quality of life.
- the predicted changes in general and internally experienced complaints, and in quality of life 
in the KIKAN intervention group will be comparable to the changes in outpatient psychotherapy without KIKAN.
2. Concerning other clinical measures. We hypothesize that:
- the children’s self‑efficacy and emotion-regulation abilities will improve over the course of KIKAN‑supported therapy.
3. Concerning app‑related data. We hypothesize that:
- changes in the therapeutic outcomes, as well as in other clinical measures and therapy‑process variables, will be associated with app‑related data (gaming data, EMA data, and acceptance of KIKAN).
4. Concerning acceptability and feasibility. We hypothesize that:
- EMA data collection and the KIKAN game will be accepted by the children, their caregivers, and their therapists.
- children and caregivers will rate the KIKAN app as user‑friendly and subjectively effective.
- the KIKAN intervention will be feasible (e.g., recruitment goals are met, participants complete the intervention, and participants use the app regularly).

To test the hypotheses regarding the therapeutic outcomes and additional clinical measures, we will compare the values obtained at the start of the intervention with those at the end of the intervention. The primary therapeutic outcomes (excluding anxiety symptoms, because no comparator data are available) for the KIKAN group will also be compared with existing data from patients who received therapy without KIKAN. In further analyses, the most important therapeutic outcomes will be examined for associations with other outcome and process variables, with acceptance and feasibility indicators, and with EMA metrics and game related variables. 
Moreover, app related variables will be correlated with additional clinical measures and therapy process variables. Acceptance and feasibility indicators will be explored descriptively.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1) Child’s age ≥ 6 and ≤ 12 years.
2) Sufficient German language skills of both the child and the parent/legal guardian(s).
3) Mental disroder in which anxiety symptoms are predominant (e.g., anxiety disorder of childhood‑adolescence or emotional disorder of childhood; see ICD‑10 codes F40, F41, F93, F92.8, F94.0).
4) Written informed consent from all parent(s) or legal guardian(s).
5) The child is affiliated with the outpatient psychotherapy clinic at Osnabrück University.
Exclusion criteria:
1) The child has a neurological or other somatic disorder that affects the nervous system.
2) The child has a comorbid disorder of any of the following types:
Eating disorders (ICD‑10 F50)
Mental and behavioural disorders due to psycho‑active substances (ICD‑10 F10–F19)
Internet‑use disorder (according to DSM‑5 research criteria)
Schizophrenia, schizotypal and delusional disorders (ICD‑10 F20–F29)
Manic episode (ICD‑10 F30)
Bipolar affective disorder (ICD‑10 F31)
Dissociative disorders (ICD‑10 F44)
Intellectual disability (ICD‑10 F70–F79)
Pervasive developmental disorders (ICD‑10 F84)
3) Acute suicidality (suicidal ideation or intent).
4) Inability to play the game (e.g., severe visual impairment).
